specPoints.text: explain why substances with a simple molecular structures are gases or liquids, or solids with low melting and boiling points the term intermolecular forces of attraction can be used to represent all forces between molecules
explain why the melting and boiling points of substances with simple molecular structures increase, in general, with increasing relative molecular mass
explain how the structures of diamond, graphite and C60 fullerene influence their physical properties, including electrical conductivity and hardness
know that covalent compounds do not usually conduct electricity

primer.text: From the earlier Covalent Bonding notes you know that non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons in strong covalent bonds. This note looks at what happens between whole molecules: why the forces there are weak, why that makes melting points low, how bigger molecules push the boiling point up, and why covalent substances rarely conduct.

lessons.title: Simple molecular structures & C60 fullerene
lessons.opening: Simple molecular substances hold their atoms together with strong covalent bonds, but the forces acting between neighbouring molecules are weak. That split explains their behaviour: little energy is needed to pull separate molecules apart, so most are gases or liquids at room temperature, or solids that melt easily. C60 fullerene belongs here too, as a simple molecular structure built from sixty carbon atoms.
keyPoints: Simple molecular structures have strong covalent bonds inside each molecule but weak forces between neighbouring molecules.
The weak intermolecular forces need only a little energy to overcome, so melting and boiling points are low.
Most simple molecular substances are gases or liquids at room temperature; solids with low melting points are less common.
C60 fullerene is a hollow sphere of 60 carbon atoms, joining 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons like a football.
C60 cannot conduct, because its spare electrons move only within each buckyball and cannot migrate between them.

low.restatement: Inside each molecule the covalent bonds are strong, but between one molecule and the next the pull is weak. Heating shakes molecules apart from each other long before any covalent bond breaks, which is why these substances melt and boil easily. C60 fullerene fits the same story as a molecular sphere of carbon.
low.analogy: Imagine Velcro strips holding marbles together in small clusters: the marbles inside a cluster are firmly glued, but the clusters themselves pull apart with only a light tug.
low.examPointer: The classic exam line: when a simple molecular substance melts, the weak intermolecular forces break, not the covalent bonds; write that distinction explicitly.

medium.restatement: The two force scales must be kept apart: covalent bonds within molecules are strong, while the intermolecular forces between molecules are weak, so state changes cost little energy and the substances are gases, liquids, or low-melting solids. C60 fullerene extends the pattern: a molecular cage of 60 carbons whose unbonded fourth electron stays inside each cage, so no charge migrates between cages.
medium.analogy: Picture a bowl of oranges, each one wrapped tightly in string but only resting against its neighbours: the string is the covalent bonding, and the light contact between oranges is the intermolecular force.
medium.examPointer: For C60, quote both halves of the conductivity story: electrons do exist inside each buckyball, but they cannot migrate from one buckyball to another, so the substance does not conduct.

check.stem: Why do simple molecular substances have low melting and boiling points?

options.text: The weak intermolecular forces between molecules need only a little energy to overcome
options.explanation: Melting and boiling separate whole molecules, and the forces between them are weak, so little energy suffices.

options.text: The covalent bonds inside the molecules are weak
options.explanation: The covalent bonds are strong; the weakness sits between the molecules, which is what state changes overcome.

options.text: The molecules are very small
options.explanation: Size alone does not decide it; the deciding factor is the weak attraction between molecules.

options.text: The molecules carry opposite charges that cancel
options.explanation: The molecules are neutral overall; the intermolecular forces exist despite that neutrality.

check.stem: When a simple molecular substance melts, what is overcome?

options.text: The weak intermolecular forces between the molecules
options.explanation: State changes pull molecules apart from one another, and only the weak forces between them need be overcome.

options.text: The strong covalent bonds within the molecules
options.explanation: The molecules survive melting intact; their internal covalent bonds do not break.

options.text: The nuclei of the atoms involved
options.explanation: Nuclei are never disturbed by melting; the molecules separate whole.

options.text: Nothing needs to be overcome
options.explanation: Energy is still required, but it pays only for loosening the weak forces between molecules.

check.stem: In which physical states are simple molecular substances most commonly found at room temperature?

options.text: Gases or liquids, with low-melting solids being less common
options.explanation: The weak intermolecular forces let most such substances melt or boil below room temperature, or not far above it.

options.text: Solids with high melting points
options.explanation: High melting points belong to giant structures; simple molecular substances melt low.

options.text: Gases only
options.explanation: Liquids are common too, and some solids with low melting points exist.

options.text: Plasma at high temperature
options.explanation: Plasma is far outside the scope of molecular substances at room temperature.

check.stem: What is the structure of C60 fullerene?

options.text: A hollow sphere of 60 carbon atoms forming 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons
options.explanation: The buckyball shape joins 20 hexagons with 12 pentagons into a closed spherical cage.

options.text: Flat layers of hexagons that slide over each other
options.explanation: Layered hexagons describe graphite; fullerene curls into a closed sphere.

options.text: A rigid tetrahedral network of four-bonded carbons
options.explanation: A tetrahedral network describes diamond; fullerene is a separate molecule.

options.text: Long parallel tubes of paired carbon atoms
options.explanation: Hollow tubes describe some other fullerenes, but C60 itself is the soccer-ball sphere.

check.stem: Why does C60 fullerene not conduct electricity?

options.text: Its spare electrons move only within each buckyball and cannot migrate from one to another
options.explanation: Conduction needs charge that can travel across the substance, and the electrons are trapped inside their molecular cages.

options.text: It has no electrons at all
options.explanation: Each carbon atom carries electrons; the issue is their range of movement, not their existence.

options.text: Its covalent bonds block all heat and charge
options.explanation: The explanation rests on electrons being unable to migrate between buckyballs, not on bonds blocking charge.

options.text: It is a metal, and metals cannot conduct in this form
options.explanation: C60 is a molecular substance, not a metal; its conductivity story is molecular.

lessons.title: Melting point patterns & conductivity
lessons.opening: As the relative molecular mass of a simple molecular substance rises, its melting and boiling points generally rise with it. A bigger molecule contains more electrons, so there are more intermolecular forces of attraction to overcome when the substance changes state. The same molecular picture explains conduction: with no free ions or electrons to move, covalent compounds are poor conductors and common insulators.
keyPoints: Melting and boiling points of simple molecular substances rise as the relative molecular mass increases.
Bigger molecules contain more electrons, so more intermolecular forces of attraction must be overcome.
More intermolecular forces mean more heat energy is needed to change state, raising the melting and boiling points.
Covalent compounds are poor conductors because no free ions or mobile electrons exist to carry the charge.
Common insulators include the plastic coating on household wiring, rubber and wood.

low.restatement: A heavier molecule is an electron-richer molecule, and more electrons mean more intermolecular attractions, so more heat is needed to boil the liquid and the boiling point climbs. Without mobile charged particles, these substances cannot carry a current, which is why plastics and rubber insulate wires.
low.analogy: Think of two hook-and-loop sheets with more and more hooks sewn on: the larger sheet grips harder, and pulling it apart takes visibly more effort.
low.examPointer: Link the trend to electrons, not just size: stating more electrons, hence more intermolecular forces, is what earns the explanation mark.

medium.restatement: The trend rests on electron count: relative molecular mass rises with the number of electrons, and the intermolecular attractions grow with that count, so state changes demand progressively more energy. Conductivity fails for the complementary reason: the structures offer no free ions or mobile electrons, so charge cannot flow, making covalent compounds the everyday insulators.
medium.analogy: Picture ever-larger magnets scattered through two neighbouring sheets: each extra magnet adds to the total grip, and separating the sheets takes more force each time.
medium.examPointer: Expect a graph-style question on alkane boiling points: quote the increasing-mass trend and attach the electron-count reason rather than restating the trend alone.

check.stem: Why do larger simple molecular substances generally have higher boiling points?

options.text: More electrons give more intermolecular forces of attraction, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules
options.explanation: The electron count rises with molecular mass, and each extra electron adds to the intermolecular attraction.

options.text: Bigger molecules have stronger covalent bonds
options.explanation: Covalent bond strength is not the driver; the boiling point tracks the forces between molecules.
options.misconception: covalent bonds credited with the trend

options.text: Bigger molecules are heavier, and weight holds them together
options.explanation: Mass itself does not bond anything; the electron count behind the mass sets the intermolecular strength.

options.text: Larger molecules conduct more, raising their boiling points
options.explanation: Conduction is irrelevant to the boiling point; the intermolecular forces set it.

check.stem: The alkanes show a clear pattern in boiling points as molecular size increases. What is it?

options.text: The boiling point rises as the molecule gets bigger
options.explanation: The alkane family is the textbook display of the increasing-mass trend in simple molecular substances.

options.text: The boiling point falls as the molecule gets bigger
options.explanation: The trend runs the other way: bigger alkanes boil higher.

options.text: The boiling point stays constant across the family
options.explanation: The graph climbs steadily; constancy would contradict the intermolecular-forces argument.

options.text: The boiling point jumps randomly with no pattern
options.explanation: The pattern is clear and systematic, which is why the family illustrates the rule.

check.stem: Why do covalent compounds usually not conduct electricity?

options.text: They have no free ions or electrons available to move and carry the charge
options.explanation: Conduction needs mobile charged particles, and covalent structures offer neither free ions nor free electrons.

options.text: Their electrons are too heavy to move
options.explanation: Electron mass is beside the point; the electrons in covalent structures are simply not free to roam.

options.text: Their covalent bonds repel the current
options.explanation: There is no repulsion of current; the structures simply lack mobile charge carriers.

options.text: They conduct only when solid
options.explanation: Simple molecular substances fail to conduct in any state, since no charged particles free up on melting.

check.stem: Which set of everyday materials relies on the insulating behaviour of covalent substances?

options.text: Plastic wiring coating, rubber and wood
options.explanation: All three are covalent materials with no mobile charge, which is why they serve as insulators.

options.text: Copper wire, aluminium foil and steel nails
options.explanation: All three are metals, which conduct through delocalised electrons.

options.text: Salt solution, dilute acid and seawater
options.explanation: These conduct through dissolved ions; they are not covalent insulators.

options.text: Graphite electrodes and lead solder
options.explanation: Graphite conducts along its layers, and solder is metallic; neither is an insulator.

check.stem: Sulfur hexafluoride is a dense gas used around electrical transformers. Why?

options.text: It is a covalent substance with no freely moving charged particles, so it acts as an insulator
options.explanation: The gas's covalent molecules carry no mobile charge, which is exactly the property an insulating surround needs.

options.text: It conducts electricity away from the transformer
options.explanation: The gas is valued for not conducting; it insulates rather than drains charge.

options.text: It is metallic and therefore safe
options.explanation: It is a molecular gas, not a metal; safety here comes from insulation.

options.text: Its density makes it a conductor at high pressure
options.explanation: Density affects insulation quality, not conduction; the molecules still carry no mobile charge.

glossary.definition: Describing the forces that act between neighbouring molecules, as opposed to the bonds inside them.
A molecular form of carbon built as hollow spheres or tubes; C60 is the football-shaped first example.
The total of the relative atomic masses in a molecule, which tracks its number of electrons.
A material that does not conduct electricity, because it has no mobile charged particles.
A substance that speeds a reaction while being unchanged itself; fullerenes can hold catalysts on their surfaces.
